title: Proposal - COFINFAD Analytics
text:
Proposal - COFINFAD Analytics




PROJECT PROPOSAL
Democratizing Fintech Analytics
A Visual Analytics Approach to Customer Lifecycle and Transactional Behavior in Colombia
Team 13 — Ji Guofang  |  Lin Yan  |  Nguyen Trong Nhan







SECTION 01
Motivation

Colombia's fintech sector has grown rapidly, with digital financial services expanding across diverse demographic segments and regions with varying levels of financial inclusion. For fintech operators, the ability to understand who their customers are, how they transact, and when they are likely to leave is critical for sustaining growth. Yet for many non-technical business users, the analytical tools to answer these questions remain locked behind programming expertise and complex statistical software.
This project addresses that gap. Using the Colombian Fintech Financial Analytics Dataset (COFINFAD), we will build an interactive R Shiny application that transforms raw financial data into accessible, visual business intelligence. The application is designed around a single analytical thread: understanding what drives customer churn by examining transactional behavior, identifying behavioral segments, and modeling churn risk — all within a unified, interactive environment that requires no coding from the end user.





SECTION 02
Objectives
The project follows a coherent analytical narrative: we first explore what is happening in the data (Module 1: EDA & CDA), then ask why by grouping customers into behavioral segments (Module 2: Clustering), and finally predict what will happen by modeling churn probability (Module 3: Predictive Modeling). The eight key observations below are deliberately sequenced along this narrative arc.





query_stats

Module 1: Exploratory & Confirmatory Data Analysis



Observation 1 — Seasonal transaction volume patterns differ by transaction type
By plotting monthly total transaction amounts as interactive line charts, faceted or color-coded by type (Transfer, Withdrawal, Payment, Deposit), we expect to uncover distinct seasonal peaks. For example, Transfers may spike at year-end while Deposits may be steadier. This gives analysts a first look at when financial activity concentrates and which channels drive volume.


Observation 2 — Transaction behavior varies significantly across income brackets and acquisition channels
Using ANOVA and Welch's T-tests on the mean transaction value (avg_tx_value) grouped by income_bracket (Low, Medium, High, Very High) and acquisition_channel (Organic, Referral, Paid Ad, Partnership), we will test whether observed differences are statistically significant. The Shiny app will display interactive box plots alongside p-value summaries, enabling users to select any grouping variable and dependent variable for confirmatory testing.


Observation 3 — Customer demographics cluster geographically across Colombian regions
A choropleth map of the 15 Colombian departments in the dataset will visualize spatial distributions of customer counts, average income bracket, and average churn probability. This helps analysts identify regions where the fintech service is over- or under-penetrated and where churn risk is geographically concentrated.








hub

Module 2: Customer Behavior Clustering



Observation 4 — Customers form distinct behavioral segments based on transactional metrics
Using pre-computed customer-level features (tx_count, avg_tx_value, total_tx_volume, weekend_transaction_ratio, customer_tenure, credit_utilization_ratio), we will perform cluster analysis to segment the 48,723 customers. The key segmentation variables are chosen to capture the Recency-Frequency-Monetary (RFM) dimensions plus behavioral volatility.


Observation 5 — The optimal number of clusters can be determined visually
The Shiny app will display an elbow plot (within-cluster sum of squares vs. k) and a silhouette plot to help users select the appropriate number of clusters. These diagnostic plots will update dynamically as users adjust the feature inputs.


Observation 6 — Cluster membership correlates with demographic and product characteristics
Once clusters are formed, linked bar charts will show the demographic composition (income_bracket, acquisition_channel, clv_segment) of each cluster. PCA scatter plots color-coded by cluster will reveal separation in the reduced feature space. This cross-referencing allows analysts to build intuitive profiles: for example, “Cluster 2 is dominated by high-income, low-frequency users acquired through partnerships.”








psychology

Module 3: Churn Prediction & What-If Simulation



Observation 7 — A small set of features dominates churn prediction
Using a pre-trained logistic regression model with Lasso (L1) regularization, the app will display a variable importance plot showing which features most strongly predict churn_probability. Users can adjust the regularization penalty (λ) via a slider to see how the model progressively drops less important variables, providing an intuitive understanding of feature relevance.


Observation 8 — Changing specific customer attributes meaningfully shifts predicted churn risk
A What-If simulator panel will allow users to input hypothetical customer profiles (e.g., adjusting tx_count, avg_tx_value, customer_tenure, credit_utilization_ratio) and see the predicted churn probability update in real time. This enables business users to answer questions like: “If we increase a customer's active_products from 1 to 3, how much does their churn risk drop?”







SECTION 03
Data
The project uses the Colombian Fintech Financial Analytics Dataset (COFINFAD), consisting of two relational tables linked by customer_id:

Records
Variables
Key Fields

3.1 Why the Transaction Log Needs Aggregation
The raw transaction log contains 3.15 million rows. Loading this directly into a Shiny application is not feasible for interactive use — every user interaction (filtering, plotting) would require processing millions of rows, resulting in response times of several seconds or more. Therefore, we aggregate the transaction log into two derived tables during data preparation:




calendar_month
Aggregation 1: Monthly Summary

For Module 1 (Temporal EDA). Group by month and transaction type, computing total_amount, tx_count, and avg_amount.
Collapses 3.15M rows → 48 rows (12 months × 4 types), enabling instant rendering of time-series charts.



person
Aggregation 2: Customer-Level Features

For Module 2 (Clustering). Group by customer_id and pivot transaction types wider, computing: total amount and count for each of the 4 types (8 features), spending_volatility, weekend ratio, and recency.
Most features already exist in customer_data.csv; this aggregation validates and adds per-type breakdowns.




3.2 Data Cleaning and Imputation
The credit_utilization_ratio column has 37.5% missing values (18,263 of 48,723 records). We will handle this with median imputation grouped by income_bracket, since credit utilization patterns likely differ across income levels. All cleaning steps will be documented on the project website with analytical rationale, not just code.




SECTION 04
Methodology









4.1 Module 1: Exploratory & Confirmatory Data Analysis




show_chart Visualizations

•Time-series line chart: Monthly total transaction amount, filterable by transaction type. Built with ggplot2 + plotly for hover tooltips and zoom.
•Choropleth map: Customer count, average churn probability, or average CLV by Colombian department. Built with tmap for interactive spatial exploration.
•Distribution plots: Histograms and box plots of avg_tx_value, tx_count, and customer_tenure, grouped by user-selected categorical variable.



calculate Statistical Tests

•ANOVA: To test whether mean transaction values differ across income brackets (4 groups) or occupations.
•Welch's T-test: For pairwise comparisons between two selected groups (e.g., Organic vs. Referral acquisition channels).
•Test results (F-statistic, p-value, effect size) will be displayed in a summary panel beside the corresponding plot.








4.2 Module 2: Customer Behavior Clustering



Why Not Run K-Means Live in Shiny?
Running K-Means clustering on 48,723 records with multiple features on every user interaction is computationally expensive. Interactions should respond in under one second.
Our Approach: Pre-compute + Visual Exploration

•Pre-compute clusters offline: Run clustering for k = 2 to 8 on standardized features, store labels as columns (cluster_k2, cluster_k3, …, cluster_k8).
•User selects k via slider: The app reads pre-computed labels instantly — no re-computation needed.
•User selects PCA axes: PCA is also pre-computed. The scatter plot re-renders instantly.



Clustering Methods


K-Means
Fast, well-suited for roughly spherical clusters. Hartigan-Wong algorithm via R's stats::kmeans(). Diagnostic: elbow plot and silhouette scores.


Hierarchical (Ward's)
Produces a dendrogram revealing nested cluster structure. hclust() with method = "ward.D2", cut at different k values.


PAM (Medoids)
More robust to outliers than K-Means. Uses actual data points as cluster centers. Particularly relevant for financial data with extreme transaction amounts.



Feature Selection for Clustering

tx_count
avg_tx_value
customer_tenure
weekend_transaction_ratio
credit_utilization_ratio
active_products

The UI presents named presets (“RFM Features”, “Full Behavioral Features”, “Engagement Features”) alongside a custom option that triggers a brief re-computation with a loading spinner.





4.3 Module 3: Churn Prediction & What-If Simulation




Model Specification
Dependent variable: churn_probability (continuous, 0 to 1). Treated as a regression problem using regularized linear models.
Independent Variables:

Transactional: tx_count, avg_tx_value, total_tx_volume, monthly_transaction_count, transaction_frequency, weekend_transaction_ratio, avg_daily_transactions
Demographic: age, household_size, income_bracket (dummy-encoded), customer_tenure
Engagement: active_products, app_logins_frequency, feature_usage_diversity, credit_utilization_ratio, satisfaction_score, nps_score, support_tickets_count, resolved_tickets_ratio



Modeling Approach
We use glmnet in R to fit regularized regression models:

•Lasso (L1): Performs automatic variable selection by shrinking less important coefficients to exactly zero. Primary model for feature importance.
•Ridge (L2): Retains all variables but shrinks coefficients proportionally. Comparison model to validate Lasso selections.

Pre-trained offline using cv.glmnet() with 10-fold cross-validation. Saved as .rds file loaded at Shiny startup.



Feature Engineering


product_diversity_ratio
active_products / 5 (max possible products)


ticket_resolution_gap
support_tickets_count × (1 − resolved_tickets_ratio)


satisfaction_gap
base_satisfaction − satisfaction_score



Shiny Interactivity

•Variable importance plot: Horizontal bar chart of absolute Lasso coefficients at user-selected λ.
•λ slider: Users adjust the regularization penalty to see how the model simplifies — teaching the bias-variance tradeoff visually.
•What-If panel: Users input feature values via sliders and dropdowns. The app calls predict() on the pre-trained glmnet model and displays predicted churn probability as a gauge chart in real time.






SECTION 05
Prototype Sketches


The COFINFAD Shiny application is built with a navbar-based multi-page layout powered by bslib. Each module occupies its own tab within a top-level navigation bar, and every tab follows a consistent sidebar + main panel pattern — the sidebar provides analytics calibration controls (filters, sliders, dropdowns) while the main panel displays responsive output panels. All heavy computation is done offline; the app only loads pre-processed data and pre-trained models.


dashboard 5.1 Shiny Layouts & Components





Layout Architecture
The outermost shell of the application is bslib::page_navbar(), which renders a fixed top navigation bar with the COFINFAD brand title on the left and three clickable tabs — EDA & CDA, Clustering, and Prediction — on the right. The theme argument is set to bs_theme(bootswatch = "darkly") to apply a dark colour scheme across all panels.
Each tab is created with bslib::nav_panel(). Inside every nav_panel(), a bslib::layout_sidebar() splits the view into a left sidebar (approximately 300 px wide) that holds all analytics calibration controls, and a main content area on the right that displays the output panels.
Within the main content area, bslib::layout_columns() with col_widths = c(6, 6) arranges output panels into a responsive two-column grid. Each individual panel (chart, table, or statistics card) is wrapped in a bslib::card() with a card_header() that labels the visualization (e.g., "Monthly Transaction Volume", "PCA Scatter Plot", "Churn Probability Gauge").




Calibration Input Components

dateRangeInput() — placed in the Module 1 sidebar; allows users to select a start and end month to filter the time-series line chart of monthly transaction volume, so that seasonal or trend patterns can be examined at different time windows.
shinyWidgets::pickerInput() — used for multi-select dropdowns throughout all three modules. In Module 1, it filters customers by income bracket and segment. In Module 2, it selects which behavioural features to include in the clustering algorithm. The multiple = TRUE and live-search options let users search and select from long feature lists.
checkboxGroupInput() — placed in Module 1 to toggle which transaction types (Transfer, Withdrawal, Payment, Deposit) are included in the EDA charts and statistical tests.
selectInput() — used in Module 1 for choosing the grouping variable (e.g., income_bracket, customer_segment) and dependent variable (e.g., avg_tx_value, tx_count) that feed into the ANOVA / T-test, as well as the choropleth map metric.
sliderInput() — in Module 2, controls the number of clusters k (range 2–8) to recalculate the clustering in real time. In Module 3, controls the regularization penalty λ for Lasso/Ridge, and also drives the What-If scenario panel where each customer attribute (tx_count, avg_tx_value, customer_tenure, credit_utilization_ratio, satisfaction_score, etc.) has its own slider so users can simulate hypothetical customer profiles and see the predicted churn probability update instantly.
radioButtons() — in Module 2, switches between K-Means, Hierarchical, and PAM algorithms. In Module 3, toggles between Lasso and Ridge regularization models. Each selection triggers a reactive recalculation of the corresponding output panels.





Output Components

plotly::plotlyOutput() — renders the interactive time-series line chart (Module 1), PCA scatter plot colour-coded by cluster (Module 2), elbow and silhouette diagnostic plots (Module 2), variable importance bar chart, and cross-validation λ-vs-MSE curve (Module 3). Plotly provides hover tooltips, zoom, and brush selection across all charts.
leaflet::leafletOutput() — renders the choropleth map of Colombian departments in Module 1, coloured by the user-selected metric (customer count, average churn probability, or average CLV). Users can zoom, pan, and click on departments to see detailed tooltips.
DT::DTOutput() — displays the cluster summary statistics table in Module 2 (mean of each feature per cluster) and the current-vs-hypothetical comparison table in Module 3. Both tables are sortable, searchable, and paginated.
uiOutput() — used for the statistical test result panel in Module 1 (dynamically renders test statistic, p-value, effect size, and interpretation) and the churn probability gauge in Module 3 (a reactive HTML gauge that updates as What-If sliders change).






draw 5.2 Wireframe Sketches
Each wireframe shows the sidebar calibration controls on the left and the output panels on the right, illustrating how users interact with the analytics.



Module 1: EDA & Confirmatory Data Analysis




How the user interacts with this tab:

The user opens the app and lands on the EDA & CDA tab. The sidebar on the left presents all filtering and analysis controls.
Using the date range picker, the user narrows the time window (e.g., 2023-01 to 2023-06) — the time-series line chart on the right immediately updates to show monthly transaction volume for that period only.
The user then uses the income bracket and customer segment multi-select dropdowns to filter the dataset (e.g., selecting only "High Income" and "Power" customers). All four output panels reactively refresh to reflect the filtered subset.
To check which transaction types matter, the user toggles the transaction type checkboxes (e.g., unchecking "Deposit" to focus on outgoing transactions).
For confirmatory analysis, the user selects a statistical test (ANOVA or T-test), picks a grouping variable (e.g., income_bracket) and a dependent variable (e.g., avg_tx_value). The statistics result card instantly displays the test statistic, p-value, effect size, and a plain-language interpretation.
On the choropleth map, the user switches the map metric dropdown (e.g., from "customer count" to "avg churn probability") to explore geographic patterns across Colombian departments.






Module 2: Customer Segmentation (Clustering)




How the user interacts with this tab:

The user navigates to the Clustering tab. The sidebar presents controls for calibrating the segmentation analysis.
First, the user selects a feature preset from the dropdown (e.g., "RFM Features" for recency-frequency-monetary, or "Full Behavioral" for all features). This determines which customer attributes are fed into the clustering algorithm.
The user then chooses a clustering algorithm via radio buttons — K-Means, Hierarchical, or PAM. The elbow plot, silhouette plot, and PCA scatter plot all recalculate reactively to show results for the selected method.
Using the k slider (range 2–8), the user experiments with different numbers of clusters. As the slider moves, the PCA scatter plot re-colours the data points, the silhouette plot updates to show cluster cohesion, and the summary table refreshes with new per-cluster means — allowing the user to visually compare which k produces the most meaningful segments.
The user adjusts the PCA axis selectors (e.g., switching from PC1 vs PC2 to PC1 vs PC3) to view the clusters from different angles in the reduced-dimension space.
The cluster summary table at the bottom shows the mean of each feature per cluster, helping the user interpret and label each segment (e.g., "high-value loyal customers" vs. "at-risk low-engagement customers").






Module 3: Churn Prediction (What-If)




How the user interacts with this tab:

The user navigates to the Prediction tab. The sidebar is split into two sections: model calibration at the top and the What-If scenario panel below.
In the model calibration section, the user selects a model type (Lasso or Ridge) via radio buttons. The variable importance bar chart and cross-validation plot update to show results for the chosen regularization method.
The user drags the λ slider to adjust the regularization penalty. The CV performance plot (showing λ vs. MSE) highlights the current λ position, and the variable importance chart updates to reflect which customer features remain significant at that penalty level — helping the user understand the bias-variance tradeoff.
In the What-If scenario panel, the user builds a hypothetical customer profile by adjusting individual sliders: tx_count, avg_tx_value, customer_tenure, active_products, credit_utilization_ratio, satisfaction_score, nps_score, etc. Each slider represents one customer attribute.
As the user moves any slider, the churn probability gauge on the right updates in real time — for example, increasing support_calls from 2 to 8 might push the predicted churn probability from 24% to 67%, showing the user exactly which factors drive churn risk.
The comparison table at the bottom displays the current slider values side-by-side with the baseline customer profile, making it easy to see what was changed and how it affects the prediction.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Customer Segmentation Module Prototype
text:
The COFINFAD (Colombian Financial Inclusion & Fintech Analytics Database) project aims to democratize fintech analytics for Colombia’s financial ecosystem. The dataset comprises 48,723 customers and over 3.16 million transactions spanning a 12-month observation period, with 54 variables capturing demographics, transaction behavior, product usage, satisfaction, and churn probability.
Customer segmentation — the process of dividing a customer base into distinct groups sharing similar characteristics — is foundational to modern fintech strategy. As Wedel and Kamakura (2000) note, effective market segmentation enables firms to move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches toward targeted, data-driven interventions. In the Colombian fintech context, where financial inclusion remains a key policy objective, identifying underserved segments can directly inform product development and outreach strategies.



As Team 13’s Clustering module and About page owner, my responsibility covers the complete customer segmentation pipeline — from feature selection and algorithm evaluation through interactive visualisation — as well as the application’s About page. This prototype focuses on the Customer Segmentation module. The module enables analysts to:

Discover distinct behavioral groups using multiple clustering algorithms
Validate segment quality through diagnostic metrics (Elbow, Silhouette)
Profile segments by comparing feature distributions and demographic composition
Export segment assignments for downstream analysis




This report documents my work on the Customer Segmentation module in four parts:

R package evaluation — I downloaded and experimented with multiple candidate R libraries for clustering, PCA visualisation, and cluster diagnostics, then compared them and justified my selections
R code prototyping — I wrote working R code that produces correct visual outputs for every chart planned in the module
Parameters and outputs — I determined which model parameters and analytical outputs to expose on the Shiny application
UI component selection — I selected appropriate bslib/Shiny widgets for the controls and outputs identified above

Weakness: Only spherical clusters, sensitive to outliers, centroid is a synthetic mean point.

# CLARA on full data (sampling-based PAM)
set.seed(42)
t_clara <- system.time(clara_res <- clara(sc_full, k = 4, metric = "euclidean",
                                            samples = 50, sampsize = 500))

CLARA (full 48723 rows):


Show code

Show code

Key finding: PAM takes 2.66 sec on just 3,000 rows — extrapolating to 48K would require ~681 seconds. CLARA solves this by repeatedly subsampling (50 subsets × 500 rows each), running PAM on each subset, and keeping the best result.






ImportantDecision: CLARA over PAM for Large Data



For the 48,723-customer dataset, standard PAM is infeasible. CLARA (Clustering LARge Applications) from the cluster package provides PAM-quality medoid-based clustering in seconds. This is why I chose clara() as the third algorithm option in my Shiny app alongside K-Means and Hierarchical.

Scalability problem: dist() creates an n×n matrix. For 48K rows, that’s 48K² ≈ 2.3 billion entries (~18 GB RAM). My solution: subsample 8,000 rows → build tree → cutree → assign remaining points to nearest centroid. This 2-stage approach preserves Ward’s variance-minimization logic while fitting in memory.

WarningWhy DBSCAN Was Not Selected



With eps=0.5, DBSCAN finds only 1 cluster — it cannot separate customers into distinct segments because the behavioral features form a continuous distribution without clear density gaps. This reveals the fundamental mismatch:

Cannot discover segments: The k-NN distance plot shows no sharp “elbow” — there is no natural eps threshold that separates customers into distinct density-based groups. Lowering eps further would fragment the data into many tiny clusters with excessive noise
No k parameter: Users cannot specify the desired number of segments — a core requirement for my interactive Shiny module where analysts adjust k via a slider
eps sensitivity: Small changes in eps swing results from 1 giant cluster to hundreds of fragments with massive noise — this instability is unacceptable for a production dashboard

DBSCAN excels for spatial/geographic data with natural density gaps, but customer behavioral features (continuous, overlapping distributions) rarely exhibit the clear density boundaries it requires.

NoteNbClust Recommends k=3, Default Set to k=4



NbClust’s majority vote favours k=3, but I set the Shiny module default to k=4 for two reasons: (1) the elbow plot shows the sharpest WSS drop at k=3→4 (the “elbow”), suggesting k=4 is where marginal gains diminish — a complementary signal to silhouette-based indices; (2) k=4 produces segments with clearer business interpretability (high-value active, moderate-tenure, new/low-engagement, and at-risk) whereas k=3 merges two distinct behavioral profiles. Pre-computed WSS/Silhouette values are already stored in cluster_precomputed.rds (computed once in data_prep.R). The Shiny app just reads and plots — no redundant recomputation at runtime

base R plot() renders in <5ms vs ggplot2’s ~200ms — important for responsive UI
NbClust is valuable for offline analysis but too slow and verbose for interactive use

2.4 Cluster Profile Visualisation: Package Comparison

2.4.1 Option A: fmsb::radarchart (Spider/Radar Chart)


Show code
# Prepare data for radar chart
raw <- cluster_pre$raw_features
labels_k4 <- pc$methods$kmeans$labels[, "k4"]
feat_df <- raw %>% select(all_of(pc$features))
feat_df$cluster <- labels_k4

cm <- feat_df %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), mean), .groups = "drop")

# Min-max normalize
cm_norm <- cm %>%
  select(-cluster) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~(. - min(.)) / (max(.) - min(.) + 1e-10)))

# fmsb requires max/min rows at top
radar_df <- rbind(rep(1, ncol(cm_norm)), rep(0, ncol(cm_norm)), cm_norm)
colnames(radar_df) <- gsub("_", " ", colnames(radar_df))

colors <- c("#f97316","#a855f7","#fbbf24","#fb7185")
radarchart(radar_df,
           pcol = colors, pfcol = adjustcolor(colors, 0.15),
           plwd = 2, plty = 1,
           cglcol = "#aaaaaa", cglty = 1, cglwd = 0.5,
           axislabcol = "#666666", vlcex = 0.8,
           title = "Cluster Feature Profiles (Radar)")
legend("topright", paste("Cluster", 1:4), col = colors, lwd = 2,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8)








Figure 8: fmsb::radarchart — radar chart for cluster profiles





Pros: Compact multi-variable comparison, visually distinctive. Cons: As noted by Few (2012), radar charts are perceptually misleading — the area enclosed by polygon lines does not correspond to any meaningful quantity, and angular position makes precise value comparison difficult. Poor for >5 variables.


2.4.2 Option B: Heatmap (ggplot2 geom_tile)


Show code
cm_long <- cm %>%
  select(-cluster) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~(. - min(.)) / (max(.) - min(.) + 1e-10))) %>%
  mutate(cluster = factor(cm$cluster)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cluster, names_to = "feature", values_to = "normalized") %>%
  mutate(feature = gsub("_", " ", feature))

ggplot(cm_long, aes(x = cluster, y = feature, fill = normalized)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(normalized, 2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#a855f7", mid = "#1a1a2e", high = "#f97316",
                        midpoint = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Cluster", y = NULL, fill = "Normalized") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())








Figure 9: Heatmap approach — cluster × feature matrix





Pros: Clear matrix layout, precise values visible, scales well with features. Cons: Harder to compare a single feature across clusters (requires scanning a row), no interactive tooltips.


2.4.3 Option C: Grouped Horizontal Bar (My Selection)


Show code
ml <- cm %>%
  select(-cluster) %>%
  mutate(cluster = factor(cm$cluster)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cluster, names_to = "var", values_to = "val") %>%
  group_by(var) %>%
  mutate(sv = (val - min(val)) / (max(val) - min(val) + 1e-10)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(dn = gsub("_", " ", var))

p_prof <- ggplot(ml, aes(
  x = reorder(dn, sv, FUN = max), y = sv, fill = cluster,
  text = paste0("Cluster ", cluster, " | ", dn,
                "\nNormalized: ", round(sv, 2),
                "\nRaw mean: ", round(val, 2)))) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#f97316","#a855f7","#fbbf24","#fb7185")) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Normalized Value (0=min, 1=max)", fill = "Cluster") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggplotly(p_prof, tooltip = "text")








Figure 10: Grouped horizontal bar — my selected approach for cluster profiling










TipWhy Grouped Bar Was Selected Over Radar and Heatmap












Criterion
Radar (fmsb)
Heatmap (geom_tile)
Grouped Bar (ggplot2+plotly)




Perceptual accuracy

Good (color encoding)
Best (position encoding)


Interactive tooltips
No
No
Yes (raw + normalized)


Cross-cluster comparison
Overlapping polygons
Scan rows
Side-by-side bars


Academic support
Criticized by Few (2012)
Acceptable
Recommended by Munzner (2014)


plotly compatibility
No

Position encoding (bar length) is the most perceptually accurate visual channel for quantitative comparison (Munzner, 2014). The grouped horizontal bar allows direct side-by-side cluster comparison for each feature, with plotly tooltips providing both normalized and raw values on hover.

4.4 Small Cluster Merging: Before vs After
A key technical contribution is automatic merging of micro-clusters (<1% of total customers) into their nearest large cluster:

# Apply merge function
merge_tiny_clusters <- function(labels, sc, min_pct = 0.01) {
  n <- length(labels)
  tab <- table(labels)
  tiny <- as.integer(names(tab)[tab < n * min_pct])
  if (length(tiny) == 0) return(labels)
  big <- as.integer(names(tab)[tab >= n * min_pct])
  if (length(big) == 0) return(labels)
  cen <- sapply(big, function(i) colMeans(sc[labels == i, , drop = FALSE]))
  for (ti in tiny) {
    pts <- which(labels == ti)
    cent_ti <- colMeans(sc[pts, , drop = FALSE])
    nearest <- big[which.min(colSums((cen - cent_ti)^2))]
    labels[pts] <- nearest
  }
  as.integer(factor(labels, levels = sort(unique(labels))))
}

raw_feat <- cluster_pre$raw_features

                      cluster = factor(merged_labels), stage = "After Merge")

Figure 15: Effect of small cluster merging — before (raw k=5) vs after (merged to k=3)





Why merge? Micro-clusters (20-30 members out of 48K) have no business value — sample sizes are too small for robust profiling, and they appear as nearly invisible dots on PCA plots. The merge assigns tiny cluster members to the nearest large cluster by centroid distance.
